The first season will consist of six 30-minute episodes. The format hails from Insight Productions, Dark Slope, and Irad Eyal (“Floor Is Lava”). In the show, kids are dropped into a giant world that “shrinks” them to two inches tall. They must work through challenges like catapulting meatballs through the air and pushing a massive skee ball down the lane of a carnival midway, utilizing teamwork and strategy skills.

"Every kid wonders what it would be like to be two inches tall, where a kitchen counter becomes a mountain and a puddle becomes a lake — ‘Shrunk' finally shows them," said Aaron Berman, Head of Originals for Kids+. "It's imaginative, it's messy, and it's unlike anything else in kids' competition TV. We're thrilled to have it join our collection of unscripted competition shows on Kids+."

The Stone family is reuniting more than two decades later to honor Diane Keaton in the sequel to " The Family Stone ."

Dermot Mulroney , who starred as Everett Stone in the 2005 holiday film, returns alongside original stars Sarah Jessica Parker and Rachel McAdams. Despite their increasingly busy schedules, Mulroney tells Variety that the actors agreed to step back into their characters' shoes to honor the memory of Keaton, who starred as the family matriarch Sybil. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Rom-Com 'Eavesdropping' Tests the Future of Scripted Social Video Movie Marketing Veteran Gerry Rich on Opening 'Iron Man,' Grappling With AI and Maintaining the Human Touch

"Diane's memory is honored in everything," Mulroney said at the premiere of "The Hunting Wives" Season 2. "I would suggest that it has a different quality than just your garden variety sequel. Maybe it's just that it's a family returning together that gives it resonance. But there's something magical about this movie."

Titled "The Families Stones," the sequel follows the Stone family 20 years after their mother's passing. As they reunite for Christmas, they're met with an unexpected surprise when their father brings home the woman he's since fallen in love with.

Photos of Mulroney on set with Parker and McAdams went viral in October and generated buzz among fans of the original film, which Mulroney said "amazed" him and his co-stars.

"It really affirmed for us how beloved that film is, as if we needed to be told again," he said. "It ripened on the vine and grew over these 21 years, and we are, right now, in the process of a very magical experience. We're riding high, just combining all of these loved ones playing loved ones. It's remarkable." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Jean Smart joins the sequel alongside returning cast Claire Danes as Julie Morton, Craig T. Nelson as Kelly Stone, Luke Wilson as Ben Stone, Tyrone Giordano as Thad Stone, Elizabeth Reaser as Susannah Stone, Paul Schneider as Brad Stevenson and Brian White as Patrick Thomas.

Mulroney was promoting the sophomore season of "The Hunting Wives," where he stars as politician Jed Banks. Although the show's first season was based on May Cobb's novel of the same name, Season 2 had no source material and is the result of the imaginations of creator, writer and showrunner Rebecca Perry Cutter and Cobb.

"They took Season 1 and went further somehow," Mulroney said. "We jumped off from that book that May Cobb wrote and made up a bunch of shit you won't believe, to be quite honest."

Recalling reading the Season 2 script for the first time, Mulroney said, "Everything I think might happen doesn't and whatever they come up with is 10 times better than anything I thought."

articles.content:
How do you wake up a 97-year-old theater? A spellbinding two-hour set from the War on Drugs .

The Philadelphia rock band headlined the Loew's Jersey Theatre on Saturday night, welcoming music fans back into the historic venue after a five-year, $130 million renovation. The grand reopening featured two sold-out concerts; the Trey Anastasio Band played on Friday.

Fans swarmed into the theater on a chilly night, marveling at its ornate ceilings and the fun, archaic features that survived the remodel — telephone booths sans telephones, a large room with a fireplace that leads into a restroom. In the auditorium, orange light bathed the Baroque vault, and red curtains hung overhead. One of the best aspects of the venue: The floor is tiered and slightly sloped, making it easier to find a vantage in the general admission area. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Rom-Com 'Eavesdropping' Tests the Future of Scripted Social Video From 'World of Warcraft Forever' Surprise to Le Sserafim, Simu Liu and T-Pain Appearances, How BlizzCon 2026 Set the Stage for Blizzard Entertainment's Next Era

After the lights dimmed, the crowd broke into eager woos and applause. And the band simmered into "Harmonia's Dream," a slow build that crests into a final refrain — "You're on your own!" — before erupting into a guitar solo, as all the best War on Drugs songs do.

Decisive piano chords ushered in "Who's That," the band's first single in five years. The audience had clearly been savoring the new song, singing along with frontman Adam Granduciel, "It's only my depression, baby!," a hook that's also printed on fresh merchandise.

"Red Eyes" was, of course, a highlight of the setlist, its euphoric rush of guitar bliss sending the crowd into a tizzy. And the climactic, 10-minute "Under the Pressure" received an applause break as saxophonist Jon Natchez fluttered around cresting synths and guitars. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Granduciel isn't a big talker during his sets, but he did take a moment to wish his mother a happy birthday. He explained that she was meant to fly down for the show but couldn't because of the FAA shutdown. As the crowd emitted a sympathetic "aww," Granduciel said, cheerfully, "So she drove down instead!"

While the new single is surely an indication, a new War on Drugs album has yet to be officially announced. But that didn't stop the band from giving fans a taste of music on the way. With zero introduction or explanation, Granduciel led the group in two unreleased songs: the power ballad "Walk Away" and the dreamy, piano-heavy "Now We're Talking."

No song was more exciting than "An Ocean in Between the Waves," its machine-like drumbeat a canvas for Granduciel to paint — his guitar a roaring, distorted beast. The song title is fitting; so much of a War on Drugs concert feels like the sea. You're drifting, lulled by currents that swell so slowly you barely notice, the band moving in tidal unison. Every so often, you spot it on the horizon: a joyous, intoxicating surge. Before you know it, you've been swept up and carried to shore.

articles.summary: Qatar will be re-signaling its ambitions to become a major international film and TV player this week with the second edition of its revamped Doha Film Festival and accompanying Industry Days, with Joe Russo and Omar Sy among the guests at the latter. The Doha Film Institute, which launched the festival under the Ajyal banner […]
articles.content:
Qatar will be re-signaling its ambitions to become a major international film and TV player this week with the second edition of its revamped Doha Film Festival and accompanying Industry Days, with Joe Russo and Omar Sy among the guests at the latter.

The Doha Film Institute, which launched the festival under the Ajyal banner in 2013, and oversees the new version, has been steadily building an ecosystem supporting local filmmakers and indie world cinema talents since its creation in 2010.

The country's Film Committee, which was created in 2022 under the auspices of Media City Qatar , is now turbo-charging efforts to connect the territory with mainstream film and TV players. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories News Festival In Focus: Doha Gears Up For Lift-Off Against Geopolitical Odds: "It's Not Smaller, We Have More Films & Guests" News Doha Film Festival Cancels 'Fing!' At the inaugural Industry Days in 2025, the committee unveiled a 50% film and TV cash rebate ; the shoot of a Barbara Broccoli-produced production of Othello starring David Oyelowo and Cynthia Erivo and partnerships with Neon, Company 3 , Miramax , Department M and Sony . Amid the buzzy atmosphere and networking chat at the event, no-one foresaw the U.S. and Israel's military campaign against Iran's Islamic Republic regime coming down the line at the end of February. The latter's retaliatory bombardment of its Gulf neighbors would temporarily bring the region to a grinding halt.

Some nine months later, hostilities have abated and Qatar is at the heart of negotiations to bring about a truce, while life has almost returned to normal amid an uneasy calm across the Gulf states.

Film Committee Hassan Al-Thawadi , who previously oversaw the organization of the Qatar World Cup, remains resolute in his drive to make the territory a key film and TV player.

"The feedback around Industry Days was very encouraging. The first edition gave us an opportunity to introduce our vision for Qatar's film industry, engage the region and hear directly from filmmakers, studios, producers and financiers," he says.

“More importantly, after the event, we understood that our vision resonated with support for the ecosystem around financing, production, talent, infrastructure and access to the region we are trying to build,” he adds. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

He acknowledges that the U.S.-Israel-Iran war has thrown up challenges but says the overall plan remains in place.

"We can't escape the difficult period our region has experienced," he says. "However, the fundamentals of what we are trying to build has not changed. We have a long-term strategy to attract international production, develop Arab talent and capability and to create a stronger platform for stories from our region to reach global audiences.”

Proof of this, is the second edition of three-day Industry Days which kicks off on Thursday, with a guest list bursting with heavy-hitters and the promise of as many announcements as the inaugural event.

“Last year was about introducing the Film Committee, our ambition to transform Qatar into a global hub for the film industry, and a new proposition for the region to create greater opportunities and international visibility for Arab cinemas. This year the emphasis is on progress and moving from ambition into activity,” says Al-Thawadi.

“The clearest evidence of progress this year is a portfolio of supported films with Paper Tiger , Artou and Furies reaching international festivals, and projects moving through creative development and production planning,” he continues.

“You will hear more about the Qatar Screen Production Incentive and how we are extending its regional reach, about projects and talent moving into their next stages, and about partnerships becoming more practical and production focused.

Among those due to attend are Squid Games creator Hwang Dong-hyuk, who will join a conversation on how the show conquered the world and Joe Russo, who is no stranger to the Gulf region.

Omar Sy will join a discussion on why actors are increasingly creating their own studios. Alongside his acting career, the Lupin star is a producer under the Carrousel Studios banner, his joint company with Thomas Benski who will also be town.

Regional talents joining the conversation include Ukraine-born, Germany-based Syrian Lebanese filmmaker Ameer Fakher Eldin ( Yunan ) who will join a conversation with Syrian star Taim Hasan and Kuwaiti journalist and media host Ammar Taqi on the challenge of bringing real lives onto the big screen.

In other panels, there will be a focus on Indonesia as Asia's Next Screen Powerhouse, while the event venue is also hosting an exhibition going behind the scenes of the making of films including Jurassic Park and Forest Gump .

The Doha Film Festival program in the meantime bears testimony to the grassroots filmmaking culture which is slowly but steadily taking shape.

In a watershed moment for the local filmmaking scene, four locally produced features – spanning Jodari Meno by Jamal Al Khanji, A Very Ordinary Life by Muhammed Deniz, First to Fly by Rodrigo Vazquez Salessi and When the News Breaks You by Hamad Al Hajri – will world premiere in the Made in Qatar section.

In documentary Jodari Meno , Qatari director Al Khanji, a trained heart surgeon and avid spearfisherman, reflects on his life and family ties while documenting his worldwide quest to catch a world record dogtooth tuna.

Turkish director Deniz's Qatari–Moroccan–Turkish feature film A Very Ordinary Life follows a retired Qatari pilot and a young Moroccan art teacher whose lives become intertwined through dreams and letters, unaware of a buried family secret.

Argentinian London-based journalist and director Vazquez Salessi's documentary First to Fly follows two young gymnasts on a quest to become the first ever athletes to represent Qatar in the Rhythmic Gymnastics World Championships. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-articleX","mid-article","btf","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() ; });

The debut feature documentary of Qatari filmmaker Al Hajri, When the News Breaks You explores the challenges facing journalists working in the Middle East.

Both Jodari Meno and When The News Breaks were made with the support of the Doha Film Institute over many years, with the directors also attending its workshops as well as its annual project and talent incubator Qumra.

"Attending events like Qumra and exposing the work to critics definitely shaped this work," says Jodari Meno director Al Khanji.

"The film started as an adventure documentary with my goal to show all this footage I had shot around the world with these strange fish and crazy encounters with sharks," he explains.

It slowly dawned him that there was also a more personal side to the story, but it took feedback from mentors at Qumra and the DFI to push him in that direction

"Someone said the underwater footage is beautiful, but you need to talk more about you," he recalls. "It's not something I would necessarily have done on my own."

Al Khanji hopes films like his will bring a fresh perspective on the region.

"The more we have people telling human stories, the better the area will be understood,” he says.

articles.summary: A week on from that buzzy finale, the co-stars, who play synthezoid Vision and his superpowered son Tommy Maximoff, tell all to THR about filming the final chapter of the ‘WandaVision’ trilogy and what that heartfelt family reunion (minus one key character) means for their futures in the MCU. "As long as there are interesting and fun stories for Vision, I’ll be putting on my tights," quips Bettany.
articles.content:
[This story contains MAJOR spoilers from the finale of VisionQuest , “Forever.”]

For all its existential theatrics, Marvel's VisionQuest was always going to tell a profoundly human love story between a synthezoid father, Vision (Paul Bettany), and the long-lost son he finally claims as his own, Tommy Maximoff (Ruaridh Mollica).

Created by Terry Matalas , the new Disney+ series picks up the threads left dangling after WandaVision and Agatha All Along , where White Vision vanished into the sky with his restored memories and Tommy's soul was reincarnated into the body of teenager Thomas Shepherd. Over the course of eight episodes, VisionQuest finds both characters wrestling with their fractured sense of identity. Vision works to piece together his humanity while keeping his paternal instincts at arm's length — fearing that acknowledging Tommy means accepting the loss of Wanda Maximoff (Elizabeth Olsen) — even as Tommy struggles to reconcile his new life with his latent super-speed and a deep longing for the family he barely remembers. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Movies 'Vision Quest' at 40: Matthew Modine Explains How the Coming-of-Age Classic Landed Him 'Full Metal Jacket' TV James Spader Returning as Ultron for Marvel's Vision Series

Vision and Tommy's parallel journeys collide in the finale, when grief pushes a newly unleashed Ultron (James Spader) — Vision's own mercurial A.I. father figure — to launch a deadly nanobot swarm on London after Jocasta (T'Nia Miller), the companion he unwittingly falls for, is killed. Rather than defeating his creator through brute force, Vision pulls Ultron into a shared sitcom mindscape — a poignant callback to WandaVision — to talk him through his pain and convince him to stand down. The gambit saves the city at the cost of Vision's own power core, leaving Tommy and his newly arrived twin brother Billy (Joe Locke) to combine their powers and revive their father, cementing the family bond Vision spent all season running from. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Having finally reclaimed his humanity (and transformed back to his original red self), Vision decides to finally release the various A.I.s from his mindscape, dismantling the internal sanctuary he once used to shut out the world so he can build a real life with his now-grown sons.

By the end of VisionQuest , Vision is "fully ready to engage with planet Earth [and] the people in it, rather than this space that he has created where he can just hide and ruminate in his own mind," Bettany tells The Hollywood Reporter . Still, the English actor — who first played the synthezoid in 2015 — insists that he doesn't know what the future holds for his character: "As long as there are interesting and fun stories for Vision, I'll be putting on my tights."

Similarly, Mollica claims that he does not know when he will play Tommy again, but he knows how his character fits into the MCU canon. "I loved the Young Avengers comics," says the Scottish-Italian actor. "I really started reading them all as I was going through the audition process for character research. Those stories are so cool, and it'd be cool to explore that one day."

In separate conversations last week, which have been edited into the extended Q&A below, Bettany and Mollica spoke to THR about playing out Vision and Tommy's parallel trajectories, sharing the screen with Locke's Billy for the first time, and their hopes for a full Maximoff family reunion.

Jac Schaeffer initially conceived WandaVision as the first show of an MCU trilogy, but she reportedly stepped away from this Vision sequel to focus on Agatha All Along , and Terry Matalas quickly stepped in to redevelop the show. Paul, what exactly was your collective vision — no pun intended — for this final installment, and how involved were you in crafting the story as an executive producer? blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

PAUL BETTANY It was actually a great thing that we had five years to figure this out. We were able to sit with ideas about what the show could be. It's easy to think of Marvel as a kind of infernal machine churning out endless product, and actually, it's very boutique in that you can count the people on one hand that you're actually speaking to about a project. When Terry came on, he and I went and had a delicious lunch, and he was very collaborative, which is in keeping with how all of my experiences with Marvel have been. He was asking what I wanted to do, and I knew that we were going to have Tommy in it and eventually Billy — it feels so weird to say because I've been keeping that so secretive for so long! ( Laughs. )

To that end, I wanted to make it really about fathers and sons. I thought it would be a really cool counterprogramming to WandaVision , which was a lot of female energy, to end it with something that was a lot of positive male energy and see how different characters deal with their grief. So when Terry said, "I have an idea. What about we get the band back together and we get James Spader?" I was like, "That's it! Because now we can do pain and trauma being passed down from father to son, but do it with robots and lasers and fighting and all of that great Marvel stuff."

Ruaridh, you didn't even know what you were auditioning for until you met Paul and Terry for a screen test in Los Angeles. How did those early conversations inform your approach to playing Tommy, given that he is also grappling with dual identities like Vision? blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

RUARIDH MOLLICA The hardest part was figuring out the inner conflict within Tommy right at the start in the first few episodes, where he is denying his existence as Tommy Maximoff, and he's very much holding onto his life as Thomas Shepherd. He grew up an orphaned kid, he's not had a lot of support and love in his life, and all he really wants to be is seen. So when you throw something else into the mix that he others himself with, it makes that harder to accept. He's really struggling with the impossibility of these nightmares that he's having.

Through those conversations, we really wanted to lean into his utter fear. In that first scene where Tommy meets Vision, I'm strapped in the chair in St. Mayben's [the psychiatric facility where Thomas Shepherd was held after Tommy's consciousness was moved into his body], and White Vision goes underneath the red light, and it makes up the red face of all of these nightmares that my character had been having. I put a picture of Paul's face as Red Vision on my wall and wrote "Devil! Nightmare!" around it, because it was so important to be afraid of him at the start.

And then it meant a really natural progression into slowly trusting and that back and forth of slowly accepting the truth. I guess we're both doing that simultaneously. To see them on such a parallel journey is really funny sometimes because they're both wanting the same thing and both unable to accept it. But that's what's so beautiful about that relationship, because they need each other to do that. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid4' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

For most of the season, Vision acts like a father to Tommy while refusing to claim the title, fearing that acknowledging his son means accepting the loss of Wanda and the destruction of their family. It isn't until he confronts that grief and embraces his humanity that he can finally step wholeheartedly back into fatherhood.

BETTANY You've identified what the whole show really is about, which is an acceptance of who you are and being cool with your identity. There is a moment where I'm with Tommy at the pool in episode three, and I tell him, "This isn't you. I just haven't been listening well enough, and you are who you think you are." I think that's a really powerful thing to say to young people.

I've had the fortune — because I've been playing this character so long — of meeting the people who are fans of that character. If you listen and you are open, you will hear what feels important about Vision to them — and I really did listen. There was a lot of similarity in the people who were fans of Vision, and I realized, "Oh, that was me when I was young. I was the bullied kid. I was the kid who didn't feel like he fit in anywhere, who was so concerned that there wasn't going to be a place for him in the adult world." And then you understand what that contract is between the audience and Vision.

So that moment foreshadows the moment where Vision finally accepts who he is and what has happened to him, which Terry and I wanted to be the moment that Vision becomes his most powerful. It's true of humans: [The moment] you really accept who you are and what has happened to you and are okay with that is when you become the most powerful version of yourself. So because we're in a superhero show with robots, that's where he gets his powers back. The initial remit from Kevin Feige was: How do we get cool White Vision back to warm Red Vision? We thought it'd be so great and a nice bit of clockwork storytelling if that is the reason that he becomes whole again. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid5' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Vision's personal breakthrough comes in episode seven, when he finally confronts the grief of losing his family — allowing him to transform back into his red self. He only reaches that point after an encounter in his mindscape with two figures whose own complicated father-son dynamic forces him to reflect on his role as a parent: Dr. Phineas Horton, the WWII-era scientist who built the first synthetic man, and J.I.M., his emotionally conflicted creation. Considering you had to play all three characters in that scene, what was the biggest challenge of acting opposite yourself multiple times?

BETTANY I'm always up for a challenge, and it was the most challenging three days mentally, but not really for the reasons one might think. I had a brilliant stunt man called John who was up for learning all of the lines, and he would play the scenes with me. But the problem is when you're working on your script, you know the story and the lines, but you don't know how the other actor is going to say those lines. It made me really relish working with actual other actors who are not me, because, for instance, [when] you're working with James Spader, there's never a scene where he doesn't do something to surprise you, and that's gold dust as an actor working opposite them. Whilst I am working opposite John, I basically know what I'm going to do when I'm the other person.

So it was a tricky three days, but it was such a laugh to know what we were trying to accomplish. There was some pressure on that scene, because it's really where you are landing the plane in terms of Vision coming to terms with who he is. The last thing we shot was White Vision's coverage. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid6' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Terry, who was directing episodes seven and eight, did a fantastic job with me. He's an actor's director, and he pushed me. It's a silly thing, right? You think of sad things and make yourself upset, and unless you're an insane person, it's hard to want to stay in that place. You get in there and you want out; you want to get the shot. I said, "I don't know, Terry. I think we've got it." He walked me around the corner and we sat down together, and he went, "I think we got it, but I was wondering: We do still have a little bit of time left, and if you have one [more]…" He was, in that very gentle way, pushing me to dig deeper — and that's the take [of Vision's breakdown] he used.

As Vision rediscovers his own powers, Tommy — whose superhero name is Speed — is also just beginning to realize that he has powers he can't control yet. Ruaridh, how did you figure out what those powers would actually look like in live action?

MOLLICA One of my favorite parts about superhero films and shows is when they're figuring out their powers and don't quite know how they work yet. At the start, it had to manifest as smaller things. So exploring how that would exist in the transference of energy from the electrical cattle prod in episode two felt like a good way to let that out first, where even Tommy's not sure what happened. It planted seeds of the truth in his psyche, but it wasn't a big enough event for him to be like, "Oh wow, I have superpowers," because it could still be played off as a freak accident. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid7' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

But it was really cool doing the one in the swimming pool with Paul when I bring him back to life, exploring how speed manifests in being able to change the molecular structure and put that atomic speed into the water to create enough electrical charge to bring him back. We did things multiple times so they'd be stacked over each other in post and used a lot of flickering light and the camera at a certain frame rate [to create that effect].

The running was great, though. When I say, "I'm Tommy Maximoff," [in the finale], that was the first time I actually sprinted. It was my favorite moment to shoot the whole show because it felt so badass, and Terry was just like, "Just fucking leg it." And I just ran ! I was like, "This is my big sprint moment. I've got to sprint." And only Terry could take the epic superhero moment and make it hilarious by having a father-son argument while running around the table .

Did you have any particular conversations about Tommy's green Adidas jacket, given that it is the closest he gets to wearing a super suit this season?

MOLLICA At the start of the show, we actually did plan to fit a superhero suit, and it was only later on as we got into the show that [we realized] Billy could create his suit because of his powers, but there was actually no way for Tommy to find a speed suit. I guess we leaned more into how Spider-Man made his first suit. We wanted to do a really strong nod to the suit and have that essence of the comic book green. Obviously, we did get our speed goggles, which are such a signature part of Speed. I think the direction of the track suit and that kind of vibe goes hand in hand with his superpower and the nod to running. It's kind of funny — of course, Tommy was like, "Wow, I'm super Speed. What would I wear? Oh yeah, running gear." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid8' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Paul, you mentioned that the plan was always to have Billy reunite with Vision and Tommy by the end of VisionQuest . Ruaridh, at what point did Terry clue you in that the twins would be reuniting and using their combined powers to save their father?

MOLLICA I didn't know before we'd started shooting or anything because I don't think those scripts had been written yet. I'm sure the ideas were already there, but it must have been almost halfway through when I found out Joe was coming back. I actually think I knew Joe was coming back before he did! ( Laughs. )

It was absolutely epic to read that in the script, but doing those scenes in real life and bringing that off of the page was just so magical — pardon the pun — because it's really a different visual language that gets brought in with Joe's character that is his signature blues and purples and witchy hexes. It was like stepping into a whole different world, which was really quite exciting. There was that really tough day where we meet each other in the hex for the first time [at the start of the finale]. It was lit by all real candles, so that was the hottest room in the world, so much so that I think me and Joe spent a lot of time laughing.

Tommy initially believes that Billy is too far away to help him, but Tommy could not save Vision alone. Can you give voice to what is going through Tommy's mind when he sees Billy come through that portal?

MOLLICA I think he just feels held and united in a way that I don't think he ever has felt before. Tommy really goes into that moment believing that he can bring Vision back. And when he can't, I think he starts to doubt his strength: "How could I possibly lose the father that I only just found?" Terry and I really agreed that Tommy should be crying in this moment. For him, he has just lost the most important person in his life that he only just found. And having Billy come in that moment to help save the day really solidifies this theme of what WandaVision was, which is that strength of family to tackle things. Obviously, for Wanda, it was to tackle her grief; in this situation, it's to resurrect. There's such beauty in that theme. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid9' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

What else do you each remember from shooting that emotional father-sons reunion?

BETTANY It was really uncomfortable. ( Laughs. ) I was wildly overacting, and my eye had been blown out from the day before or something from overacting again. [Vision's] being sort of electric shocked, I guess, to try and bring him back to life, and I was on top of that goddamn nest. ( Laughs. ) But, actually, it was a lot of fun and it felt like a moment of, the sun is shining, and [ imitates a warm hug ] God is in His heaven. I wanted it to be, as I did a lot of moments, redolent of things that people know. I think that every parent knows what it is when you've been away from your children to just be able to pull your children into you and hold onto them. So, yeah, it was a lovely moment for me.

MOLLICA That finale scene was actually my last day on the whole job. So to have Joe there for that as well was actually really beautiful, and it was quite a momentous way to end everything — and it was really powerful.

Making the show was the single most incredible and biggest moment of my whole life so far. So to have had Paul in there with me at the screen test, where I was learning about everything for the first time and finding out I got the job, and then to be with him at the end — it's just that funny thing of art imitating life. Our relationship on the show, I feel like, really reflects our relationship in real life. I am always asking Paul for advice, and I feel very supported by him as a titan of the MCU. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid10' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Paul, you recently joked that you blew a bunch of blood vessels in your eye while shooting the show, but I didn't realize that it happened toward the end of filming the finale. Were you really overacting?

BETTANY Well, you can imagine the pressure of thinking, "Okay, so I've got a device on my head that's sucking out my brain somehow. What's that going to look like?" So you do it and that's all fine, and then you realize, "Fuck! I've got to do this for six hours, or whatever." ( Laughs. ) And you're kind of going [ imitates grimacing ] for six hours. At some point, [I began] making a self-deprecating joke about wildly overacting and blowing out my eye and it being a lesson in "less is more," because I don't know how many thousands and thousands of dollars it must have cost to paint my [bloodied] eye out.

In their final scene together, Vision and Tommy talk about having dinner with Billy in Eastview. What do you imagine their lives together will look like now? How does Vision feel about having to parent his boys now as young men?

MOLLICA I think they'll just make up for so much lost time; they'll just want to be together and do regular father-son things. I imagine all the memories they had of their time in WandaVision — I think their first Halloween again together will be funny. I imagine it will still sometimes be awkward and clunky, like that scene in episode six when we're both alive [after the shootout] and I get out the back of Paladin's van, and Vision's like, "Well… I'm glad you're alright." And I'm like, "I'm glad you're alright." There's those silly, awkward moments that will always exist in that relationship because that is what family is. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid11' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

BETTANY I think right now [Vision's] thrilled and high on it all, and I'm sure the reality of all of that will cause complications. I have a similar thing that happened in my actual life when I married Jennifer [Connelly]. She already had a son. I become a sort of instant father, and that is incredibly exciting. And then the reality of it is there is a lot of work really to build that connection.

I don't know how to play a robot. I never have. I've never tried to. I always try to find human paradigms because I don't know what else to do. Vision has the problem that he seems to have a biological son in the world, but that's impossible — and yet, somehow, it is true. He has biological children. [My stepson] Kai is not mine biologically, but somehow he feels part of me — and it's just true. I feel no differently toward him than I do my actual biological children. They feel exactly the same. Some impossible osmosis has happened that we have become a part of each other. So I think I've relied very heavily on that experience for doing this fun, ridiculous notion of a robot having biological children in the world.

In their final scene together, Tommy asks Vision if he thinks there is any chance, with the two of them and Billy still around, that they may see Wanda again. Did you and the creative team ever consider bringing Wanda back for the finale? [ Writer's note: The finale features a post-credits scene — not included in press screeners — of Robert Downey Jr's Doctor Doom awakening Wanda, who had seemingly been crushed under a mountain at the end of Multiverse of Madness . ] blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid12' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

BETTANY Yes, there were conversations, and in the end, I think it was the right decision. It would seem that we have managed to make the fans care about [Vision's] journey, and for the moment he becomes most powerful to be an acceptance of what he has lost, and then to just immediately give him back [what he lost], I think could have destroyed the end of the quest for him. Because the quest in this, as it turns out, is not to find Wanda — it's to find himself. He has always been for Wanda. He's always sort of existed for her… and [a decision] was made at a high level that, "No, this is Vision's story, and it needs to finish as Vision's story." I'm (a) very flattered by that, and (b) I think it was probably the right decision. Who knows what the future [will hold]? If you tie too many of those things up, what are you going to do next?

Do you think Wanda and Vision would still work as a couple? Would they find a way back to each other?

BETTANY Well, wouldn't that be fascinating to find out? My instinct is that whilst there can be tumultuous moments, rather like Romeo and Juliet, you just have to imagine that they would. I do!

Of course, besides wanting to see Vision and Wanda back together, a lot of fans are waiting with bated breath for her to reunite with her sons. Ruaridh, you've affectionately referred to Tommy and Billy as the "queer twin brothers" of the MCU. What has it meant to you to be an openly bisexual actor playing a bisexual character on a project of this scale? blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid13' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

MOLLICA I feel so lucky (a) to be in this world of the MCU, but (b) to get to portray a character that champions the sexuality that I am as well. It's so important to have that on such a big platform that people can watch and hopefully feel seen themselves. I do think bisexual representation in big media is confusing. People don't really know how to tackle it or address it, so I feel really, really happy to be hopefully a good example for that, which is why I want to be vocal about it. Hopefully, in the future, we explore some of Tommy's other relationships that exist in the comics.

Have you talked to Joe at all about the pressure and privilege of bringing that kind of queer visibility and representation to the MCU? Does it come up in conversation often between the two of you?

MOLLICA Yeah, it totally does. He's such an important figure in queer media [because of Heartstopper ], and to be talking to him who is openly gay and has done Agatha and is in the MCU, and to have someone to ask what that is like was really important.

As if this role could not be more tailor made for you, Ruaridh, you actually earned an undergraduate degree in computer science before deciding to become an actor. Were you thinking at all about the accuracy of the coding or artificial intelligence terminology while filming the show?

MOLLICA [ Giddily ] I actually really did think about it. I would be reading the scripts trying to be like, "What have they said there? Does that make sense?" Obviously, I wanted all the code talk and things like that to make sense. For me, it was actually really reassuring because when I read it for the first time, almost all of it is based in so much truth. I'm watching it again as it's coming out and noticing all these other things and turning to my friend and going, "Yeah, that's actually how we would do that in real life." articles.title: Selena Gomez's Wondermind Fraud Lawsuit Has Been Dismissed With Prejudice
articles.summary: Investors dropped their suit against the singer, her mother and a former business partner over the mental health startup that fell apart within three years.
articles.content:
The investor fraud lawsuit against Selena Gomez , her mother Mandy Teefey and their former business partner Daniella Pierson over their mental health startup Wondermind has been dismissed with prejudice, according to a court filing submitted Tuesday.

On Monday, the plaintiffs voluntarily dismissed the suit against the three women and their company with prejudice, according to court records viewed by The Hollywood Reporter , meaning the claims against the women and how their company fell apart from this set of investors can not be refiled. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories TV 'Only Murders' Leaves the Building for London in Season 6 Trailer TV Disney Launching 'Only Murders in the Building'-Themed Escape Rooms in Cities Across the U.S. (Exclusive)

“Selena is pleased by the dismissal of the case and looks forward to putting the matter behind her,” Gomez's attorney, Mathew S. Rosengart, said in a statement to THR on Tuesday.

Two investment entities that backed Wondermind filed the suit in Delaware federal court in August. They alleged that the three women “falsely represented” that the company had the infrastructure, leadership and resources it needed, and that the roughly $1.2 million they put into it was squandered while they were kept in the dark. The complaint accused Gomez, Teefey and Pierson of securities fraud, common-law fraud and breach of contract, and asked for the investment contract to be rescinded and for damages.

According to the complaint, Gomez was pitched as central to marketing the brand, and Pierson was presented to investors as a “$200 million executive” with a “full slate of revenue-generating initiatives” already in motion.

“The partnerships did not exist. The initiatives never materialized. The app was never built,” the complaint stated. “And for three years, while the company quietly collapsed around them, not one of its founders, officers or directors said a word to the investors whose money was funding the collapse.” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

About two weeks after the suit was filed, Rosengart moved to dismiss the claims against Gomez. He argued that the plaintiffs relied on “vague, generalized, and contradictory allegations” about his client, and that she could not have committed fraud.

“Although she invested in and holds a minority stake in the company, Ms. Gomez never agreed to and did not manage the company,” the motion stated. Gomez had “agreed to support her mother, Mandy Teefey, who co-founded Wondermind,” it said. “Management was vested in Ms. Gomez's mother, Mandy Teefey, and Ms. Pierson, who ran the company as co-CEOs and board members. The company, in turn, retained Ms. Gomez as a consultant and conferred on her the title of Chief Impact Officer.”

The three women founded Wondermind, which focuses on mental fitness practices and tools, in November 2021. According to the suit, they told investors an app would be the centerpiece of the brand, supported by major advertising deals and high-profile celebrity photo shoots and cover stories.

Very little of that came to pass, and Wondermind staffers eventually began talking to the media. The investors said a story in The Cut was how they learned the company had fallen far short of what they'd been promised.

Teefey has denied accusations of company mismanagement and erratic behavior. Pierson, who left the company in 2023, "categorically denies" all of the allegations against her in the suit.

"To be clear, she has never used investor funds for personal expenses. Quite the opposite: Daniella invested her own money into the business and did not draw a salary from the company," her rep said at the time of the filing.

articles.title: The 9/11 Issue of The Amazing Spider-Man Is One of Marvel's Weirdest Moments (Especially What It Meant for the MCU's Next Big Villain)
articles.summary: Image courtesy of Marvel Comics Spider-Man has often been called the most popular Marvel hero of them all and it feels like the last few years have gone out of their way to prove that. This year, we got Spider-Man: Brand New Day, the Wall-Crawler giving Marvel Studios another billion dollar success. The Spider-Verse movies showed that the rest of […]
articles.content:
The Amazing Spider-Man (Vol. 2) was on the come up again in the early '00s. The Clone Saga had ravaged the Spider-books , and the John Byrne relaunch of the late '90s didn't work at all. In the year 2000, new Marvel editor-in-chief Joe Quesada set out to fix the problems of the previous decade, hiring Babylon 5 creator J. Michael Straczynski to take over The Amazing Spider-Man . He was able to put the book on track throughout 2000 and 2001. 9/11 was a massive shock for the world, one that every piece of pop culture had to deal with. The Amazing Spider-Man (Vol. 2) #36 would be one of the first comics to deal with the attack and it remains one of the strangest pop culture artifacts ever, especially when you think about what it meant for Doctor Doom.

9/11 is the kind of day that you never think you'll encounter in your life. One of the fun parts of fiction is that it allows you to “experience” tragedy in a safe way. Events like 9/11 feel like they came out of fiction – who would even fly a plane into a building other than some insane fictional supervillain – and we often use fiction to talk about our feelings on events like this. Fiction allows us to put our mind around the events that seem like they never would have happened and Americans in the days after 9/11 craved that.

The Amazing Spider-Man (Vol. 2) #36 dropped on November 14th, 2001, two months and three days after the disaster, from Straczynski, John Romita Jr., Scott Hanna, Dan Kemp, Richard Starkings, and Wes Abbott. The issue is simple – Spider-Man is swinging through Manhattan and witnesses the attacks, rushing to Ground Zero to help. The comic showcases various Marvel characters helping out police and fire fighters as they comb through the wreckage. There's no dialogue; it's not a story like that. Spider-Man is Marvel's most relatable hero and this issue used that to its advantage.

Straczynski used the hero as a mouthpiece for what we all were feeling at the time – the confusion, the sadness, the anger, the fear. I was able to get my hands on a copy a year or two after it come out and it is a truly gorgeous book; Romita Jr. was a lifelong New Yorker and he drew his heart out. I'm not ashamed to admit that I bawled like a baby the first time I read it. It was written to be a cathartic moment for a country that had just went through something terrible and it honestly did a good job of that.

25 years later though, it's become one of the strangest pieces of Marvel ephemera out there. To begin with, the idea that 9/11 would happen in the Marvel Universe, especially in the city where all the superheroes are, was a strange one. It sort of proved the idea that superheroes are, in the end, kind of useless. What good are they if they can't stop this sort of thing? Comics are often used as a window to the world around us, but there are times when they aren't the right lens to view things through. The Amazing Spider-Man (Vol. 2) #36 is one of those moments.

There are times when the issue seems to be hitting moments of parody, even though you can tell that it is one hundred percent earnest, especially the moments with the villains. One of the pieces of 9/11 propaganda we were sold was that it brought all of use together, so putting Magneto, Kingpin, and Doctor Doom at Ground Zero was meant to show that kind of moment. However, in the case of Doom, and to a lesser extent Magneto, 9/11 was the kind of thing that he tried to make happen on a regular basis.

We've all seen the panel where Doom is shedding tears over 9/11. It's been memed to high heaven by now and it's the moment that truly breaks the whole thing. Before this image, the issue was schmaltzy and emotional, meant to help you make sense of your feelings of the day. It was emotionally manipulative in the best possible way. However, this moment just sort of takes you out of the whole thing.

The view of 9/11 has changed a lot over the years. There was a time when people would legitimately fight you if they thought you were making light of it. Now, Gen Z makes 9/11 joke memes. Time gives us distance from all things, and that distance allows us to take a passionless look at the past. Back then, this comic was a moving, emotional moment for readers. Nowadays, it honestly feels kind of tone-deaf at times, playing on the tender feelings of a country that just wanted someone to make sense of the whole thing.

Dealing with tragedy is always a difficult thing. Every person deals with everything differently, so there's no one size fits all cure for it. In the modern day, pop culture has become a bigger part of our lives than ever and we often look to it to help us make sense of things. However, as comforting as something like The Amazing Spider-Man (Vol. 2) #36 can be, it represents the commodification of our grief. It's taking advantage of a disaster to make money for the wealthy. There's something that will always be a bit disgusting about it, even when you realize that the creators were working through their feelings as well. Therapy as commerce is always a strange thing.

Seeing Spider-Man process 9/11 will always be one of the strangest moments in comic history. Spidey's often been used as an audience surrogate, so from that perspective, this comic definitely felt right. However, there's something about the idea of a 9/11 Spider-Man comic that just feels weird. There are some interesting moments and the art is gorgeous, but there's just something about seeing a guy who one hundred percent would be celebrating if a plane hit the Baxter Building cry over 9/11 that will always make you feel kind of strange.

What do you think about The Amazing Spider-Man (Vol. 2) #36? Do you think it's strange or a stirring piece of pop cultural importance? Sound off in the comment section below.

"The Odyssey" actor Elliot Page and "Harry Potter" filmmaker Chris Columbus have signed on as executive producers of writer and director Mathew Puccini's award-winning short, "Callback."

The film is a dark comedy about a gay couple, played by Justin H. Min ("After Yang," "Beef") and Michael Hsu Rosen ("Presumed Innocent," "The Only Living Pickpocket in New York"), whose relationship unravels into competition over the course of a disastrous evening at home. The film was shot by Sam A. Davis, who won an Oscar for live-action short film for "The Singers." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories From 'World of Warcraft Forever' Surprise to Le Sserafim, Simu Liu and T-Pain Appearances, How BlizzCon 2026 Set the Stage for Blizzard Entertainment's Next Era Rom-Com 'Eavesdropping' Tests the Future of Scripted Social Video

"From the moment it begins, ‘Callback' vibrates off the screen," Page said in a statement Tuesday. "Quiet and contained, yet brimming with visceral intensity, the film is a painfully funny and incisive portrait of professional jealousy and the complex power dynamics within a relationship. It is an honor to be involved with such a gorgeously crafted film, anchored by two extraordinary performances from Justin H. Min and Michael Hsu Rosen."

Columbus said, "Matthew has directed a smart, confident and frequently hilarious film. What starts as a simple premise becomes a delightfully dangerous game of one-upmanship that kept me guessing until the very end. I immediately watched it again to savor the razor-sharp writing and superb performances. I'm so glad to have discovered Matthew's work and to play a part in spreading the word about his wonderful picture."

The film also received top honors at the San Francisco and Provincetown International Film Festivals, making it the only live-action short film this year to be 3x Oscar qualified and it has received additional honors at HollyShorts, Salute Your Shorts, Nantucket, SCAD, FilmQuest and more. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"I am incredibly grateful for Elliot and Chris' support in helping Callback to reach a wider audience," Puccini said. "This film was a true labor of love for all involved, and it's surreal to have two heroes of mine, each with their own incredible legacy of boundary-pushing work, champion our unhinged gay short."

articles.title: Could DC Be Leaving Warner Bros Along With James Gunn? The Latest Rumors
articles.summary: What does the future hold for DC Studios?
articles.content:
To say that DC Studios is in the midst of a big change would be a major understatement. It was announced a little over a week ago that in the aftermath of the Warner Bros./Paramount merger, James Gunn and Peter Safran would step down as co-CEOs of the studio. As a result, film producer (and Marvel Studios alum) Jeremy Latcham will lead the brand moving forward. There may, however, now be reason to believe that DC may be leaving WB and by extension, parent company Skydance. This is all due to some recent rumors.

Of course, all of this should be taken with a massive grain of salt, as Skydance’s David Ellison has not indicated that the company plans to sell DC Studios. If that were to actually happen, though, it would truly signify the end of an era. The DC brand has been under the ownership of Warner Bros. since 1969 and, of course, in that time, a plethora of movies, TV shows and more based around the comic book imprint have been released under WB. If Ellison and co. were to sell it, it could theoretically draw interest on the open market.

Naturally, there are a lot of unknown variables here, and it’s currently unclear as to it or when Skydance might confirm or deny the rumor that DC Studios will be sold. In the meantime, there are still film projects from the brand that are in different stages of development as James Gunn’s Man of Tomorrow is set to hit theaters on July 9 amid the 2027 movie schedule . Matt Reeves ’ The Batman: Part II is also filming right now and will hit theaters on February 18, 2028.

articles.content:
We here at ComicBook decided to do some polling on the issue and see how Bond fans were feeling. Turns out that fans are generally okay with the choice, even if they don't overwhelmingly love the choice. And considering some of the backlash that Robert Pattinson has received from previous casting announcements, that's pretty solid ground to be on, at the start.

Now that you've had the day to thinka bout it, how do you feel about Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond

Per the results of our polling, the majority of fans seem to “love” Pattinson being cast as Bond (35%). The second-highest majority (30%) seems to “like” the idea, even if they don't “love it. The third-highest group (23.4%) said that Pattinson wasn't their first choice, while only about 11% of fans said they “hate” the casting.

Again, those poll numbers are pretty solid, given what Pattinson has faced in the past. When he was cast as Bruce Wayne/Batma in Matt Reeves's reboot film, The Batman , there was some immediate backlash to it. Pattinson's physique was criticized, his past role in The Twilight Saga was dragged up and used against him, and the term “Emo-Batman” followed him well after the film's release. It's been in the four years between The Batman and the start of production on The Batman: Part II that Pattinson has seemed to gain significant clout as Batman.

Comparatively, it's looking like both males and females across many different demographics are pleased with Pattinson as Bond. Action fans can see the vision after Pattinson won them over in films like Christopher Nolan's Tenet (where he played a Bond-style spy), and as Batman; female fans haven't been shy about posting their delight at seeing Twilight ‘s Edward Cullen age into a James Bond role. Bond fan-fiction is about to go crazy .

articles.title: One of the Most Terrifying Movie Monsters Ever Created Could Soon Be Yours, For a Price
articles.summary: Courtesy of 20th Century Studios Over the last 100 years of cinema, there have been many memorable movie monsters that have burned themselves into the minds of audiences who saw them for the first time on the big screen. From slasher killers and malevolent clowns, to psychopathic androids and bloodthirsty vampires, these screen fiends have come in all shapes and […]
articles.content:
Aliens followed up Scott's intense and claustrophobia sci-fi horror movie with one of the biggest action movies of the 1980s. Two years after The Terminator , Cameron's Alien sequel asked what if the single alien threat was multiplied…and came with their even more monstrous mother. The result was a film that included huge action set pieces with dozens of aliens attacking a crew of marines and Sigourney Weaver's Ellen Ripley in a relentless thrill ride that intensified the fear but lost some of Scott's creeping terror. As with Alien , the effects used in the movie were all practical, with more men in suits being incredibly effective as the xenomorph horde. While these suits no longer hold their fear factor in their current condition and away from the lighting and director of Cameron, it would still be something to have standing among any memorabilia collection.

Practical effects come with one simple rule. If a movie looks good when it is made, then there is good chance it will not age badly like some early uses of CGI. Both Scott's original movie and Cameron's sequel turned what was a basic man in a rubber suit monster into a terrifying on-screen menace. Yet, as can be seen in the images shared and the description of the xenomorph suit used in the film, it is not quite as scary or spectacular in the flesh – or foam rubber as it were. The suit created by Stan Winston Studio based on the designs of H.R. Giger is one of only a few known to have survived, making it a rarity to come up at auction, but to look at, there has to be credit given to Cameron for managing to turn a piece of rubber and tubes into the stuff of nightmares. The whole ensemble includes a headpiece, with an inner mouth taken from another Alien movie as these suits were built without them, as well as a black spandex-blend leotard bodysuit on which is built the body of the creature from foam latex moldings, plastic tubing, and plenty of rubber attachments. Everything has been professionally restored other than the hands and feet which have been remolded from the original Stan Winston molds for this piece.

As if owning the actual suit used in the film, this has the added allure of a set of cast signatures on the base of the mannequin that comes with it. Among others, the stand has been signed by Paul Reiser, Michael Biehns, Jenette Goldstein, and Carl Troop, the performer who wore the suit in the movie. The current bid on the xenomorph is sitting at $40,000, or $60,000 with buyer's premium, but as the auction is set to run until the end of the movie it is unlikely that a piece this scarce and iconic will remain at that price when the hammer falls.

articles.summary: Moshe Rosenthal’s “Tell Me Everything” is the story of a father-son relationship fractured by an uncomfortable secret. Set in the late 1980s and early 1990s in Holon, a city in western Israel, it grapples with queerness, masculinity and family just as 12 year-old Boaz is preparing for his Bar Mitzvah. articles.content:
Moshe Rosenthal's "Tell Me Everything" is the story of a father-son relationship fractured by an uncomfortable secret. Set in the late 1980s and early 1990s in Holon, a city in western Israel, it grapples with queerness, masculinity and family just as 12 year-old Boaz is preparing for his Bar Mitzvah.

Like all Rosenthal's work, "Tell Me Everything" (his sophomore effort after "Karaoke") reflects different facets of his identity. "I don't want to let it control the story but it's just there in a way that feels organic and feels honest," he says, noting there are parallels between his own internal struggles and that of his characters. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Disney and the NFL Launch Limited-Edition Mickey & Friends Merch Ahead of Super Bowl LXI How to Watch Billy Evans' First TV Interview About 'You Can See Everything' Online

The film, which debuted at Sundance earlier this year , is now set to represent Israel at the Oscars after winning the country's top film prize at the Ophir Awards (it also broke the record for number of nominations, notching up 16 nods). Despite the reception, last month it was dropped from Swiss film festival Everybody's Perfect because Rosenthal, who hails from a Turkish and Egyptian background, is Israeli. (After threats of a boycott, Everybody's Perfect canceled two screenings despite a rep for the festival calling the work "a beautiful film about the '80s and AIDS/HIV.")

Rosenthal sat down with Variety to discuss the inception of "Tell Me Everything," its reception and what it is like to be a queer filmmaker from Israel at this moment.

I actually wrote it at the same time that I wrote my previous film "Karaoke," and it was one of those things that you feel "It's too big to be a first feature." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

I kept developing it for about eight years and it was an interesting process because, in a way — and it happens with every film — you grow up during the writing process, and the world is shifting. So with "Tell Me Everything" it felt even more important the more I worked on it, and especially when we got to a place when we were filming it. It was right during the [Hamas-Israel] war, so for us it was almost important to tell a very personal and humanistic story because there was so much hate around us. So weirdly enough, it made us very, I don't know — believe in that art.

Oh, not too long. It's it was 18 days. It was January 2025.

He was 12. My casting agent [Chamutal Zerem] showed me a picture of him and she was like, "We should see him, he reminds me of you." It takes me time to realize I'm making a film about myself so at that moment I was like, "What has that got to do with anything?"

And then I felt the responsibility of the filmmaker who meets hundreds of kids until he finds his "Elliott" [from "E.T."] and we saw a bunch of them and we got back to the first one because we knew he was special. And I think [Zerem] was right not only because he might have reminded her of me but also because he had the spirit of a director, the excitement of a film lover and a person that really wants to make great movies. That's what really connected us.

In many ways I was overly protective of him and he gave me a few times permission to be like, "I understand," but obviously there was a lot of things, especially on set. Welfare [officers] were always there, they didn't allow him to do a few things that I wanted. You're not allowed to let him smoke and there was a scene where he was holding a cigarette — that scene was deleted. His movie parents and his movie sisters were also very protective.

He's the biggest comedian [in Israel], huge. He didn't do films for 15 years… it's a combination of a comedic genius like Eddie Murphy with a Howard Hughes type of personality. He doesn't go to any parties, he doesn't go to any premieres, he doesn't go to any awards. He's very shy. Just somebody who never takes any offers when you send him a script. We sent him the script because it was one of those jokes that filmmakers do. They send him a script so he will return it because they always hope there might be a chance he'd do something, but it never happens. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Me and [Zerem], in our first meeting she was like, "Let's send it just for the sake of it [and] continue looking for somebody else" and we didn't even think about it but he immediately said yes. He saw "Karaoke" a few weeks before and he was just waiting for that call.

He's such an amazing comedian. All he does is change his masks, so when you take all the masks [away] and you see him "naked" it's like he's out of focus, it's so strange. And I felt that notion, especially for a local audience that knows him very well, could be part of that feeling, of like, "He's so close but I don't understand, I need him to just show me." And that's what we tried to do in the last scene when the two are actually communicating for the first time.

It's pretty incredible… I think I was surprised of how profound and deep the connection of the audience is to the film.

Sometimes certain films and certain type of filmmaking – and I think hopefully we've done it here — just open a door in your heart for your own memories, and that's something that is very beautiful to see. And specifically in Israel, I think it made people just remember that they have an identity and culture and a lot of things that in the last few years it's almost like we learned to put aside because we kept dealing with [geopolitical] conflicts.

I mean, it's complicated. On the one hand, I don't even think that it's only Israeli filmmakers. I think that filmmakers in general are, in a way, being forced to politicize their work, so I think it's even a bigger issue.

What I find most important, what I think I do best in a way, it's the humanistic stories that demand the viewer to not politicize it and to try to just remind people what art is supposed to be. It's supposed to create those bridges. It's supposed to allow us to have empathy for each other, and that's also part of the themes of this film. That's also what I'm trying to do with my characters. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The film deals with the consequences of shutting somebody out of your life because of [someone's identity, in this case] his sexual orientation. The consequences are terrible for both sides… The film is called "Tell Me Everything." The climax of the film is a father and son just communicating, that's it. And the ability to accept and to process, there are no easy solutions.

Yeah, I mean, I got a lot of support from other filmmakers.

But I didn't hear from the festival directly. I just read [about] their reaction. I wasn't upset as much that as I was just sad about it, and not about not being in the festival, but the fact that this is the situation. The fact that even the festival admits that [it] was bullied to not have the film, it's not even a conversation. It's just they're afraid. [Last month a representative for Everybody's Perfect told Variety the film had been deprogrammed with a "heavy heart" because "when people mention boycotting a festival that is a very big threat."]

And that's what saddens me, because it made me realize that they were actually one of those who took the film, who weren't afraid at the beginning, and took the risk, and obviously the moment that they were bullied out of their choice, I felt actually sorry for European festivals and the fact that that's the situation that we live in because I really think that it starts with one thing and it will evolve eventually. Censoring artists is not a solution for anything, and I think history proves that.

This interview is made up of two conversations, which have been edited and condensed.
